transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-11 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Sunbeam Head of Data), Evan Reed (CTO), Lara Gomez (DevOps)

Summary (auto): Quick demo of Redwood model catalog, focused on open models for document summarization and clinical note extraction. Emphasis on benchmark methodology and compatibility matrix for quantization and hardware. Next steps captured at end.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex Chen, AE at Redwood. With me is Priya Singh, our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:05] Maya: Good, thanks. Excited to see the catalog.
[00:08] Evan: Yep, thanks. We carved out 45 minutes but 42 works too.
[00:12] Priya: Cool. Quick agenda: model catalog tour, picking candidates for your summarization workload, benchmarks, and then compatibility matrices — quantization, kernel support, things like that. We'll leave time for Q&A.
[00:20] Alex: Also we'll touch on hosted vs dedicated and the Private deployment options since you mentioned compliance.
[00:25] Maya: Perfect. Our main ask — want a cost-efficient model that keeps latency under 300 ms for short notes and under 1s for longer docs, and minimal hallucinations on PHI redaction.
[00:35] Priya: Got it. Can you give a bit of context on current stack and traffic?
[00:39] Maya: Sure. We're on GCP, mix of Node backends, we currently call OpenAI for summaries — about 1k reqs/day, spike to 5k. Typical doc length ~500 tokens, sometimes 2k for long consult notes. We care about audit logs, SSO, and key management.
[00:55] Alex: Thanks. That helps. So in the catalog we'll show a few open models we think map well: a smaller 7B quantized variant for low cost and latency, and a 13B or 30B for higher accuracy on longer contexts.
[01:08] Maya: Do you have pre-benchmark numbers?
[01:11] Priya: Yes — we'll show both internal perf and cost profiles; these are estimates though. For example on A100-ish class, the 7B q4 variant is roughly 25–40 ms per token depending on batching. The 13B q4_0 is around 40–80 ms per token. But actual numbers vary with sequence length and KV cache behavior.
[01:30] Evan: Quick nit — ms per token is fine, but for whole-request latency what's typical for a 500-token doc?
[01:36] Priya: For a 500-token generation, single-request latency on hosted endpoints with streaming tends to be in the 600–900 ms range for 13B q4 if there's no heavy batching. For 7B it's more like 300–500 ms. Those are ballpark.
[01:51] Maya: That aligns with our target. Cost-wise?
[01:54] Alex: We'll include rough per-token cost in the matrix; the catalog flags models with recommended quantization profiles and expected unit costs.
[02:03] Priya: Ok jumping into the console — sorry there's a tiny typo in the transcribed deck, sometimes it says KV "cash" instead of cache — auto-transcription fun.
[02:12] (screen share noise)
[02:20] Priya: Here is the model catalog landing page — filters on size, task (summarization, chat, embeddings), recommended quantizations, and verified benchmarks. Each model card links to a compatibility matrix — shows supported kernels, recommended GPU shapes, whether the model supports Triton/FBGEMM paths and known issues like OOMs at long sequences.
[02:38] Maya: Nice. Do you annotate for hallucination rates?
[02:41] Priya: We have a quality score derived from evals — benchmark sets show metrics: rouge/emd/precision for extraction tasks and hallucination flags for clinical prompts. You can upload your prompt set and we'll run a quality check with your success criteria.
[02:56] Evan: On the compatibility matrix — is quantization tested per model? We have concerns about int8 for certain models and its effect on NER for PHI.
[03:04] Priya: Yes we include per-model quantization recommendations: q4_0, q4_k_mixed, int8 where supported. We call out when NER/regression risks are observed. For some open models we've found q4_k preserves entity recognition better, but results are model specific.
[03:20] Lara: From infra side, if we do Dedicated, what GPU shapes do you support? Also how does autoscaling work with bursts?
[03:27] Alex: Dedicated supports multiple GPU pools — A10G/A100-type shapes depending on region. Autoscaling policy is configurable with burst capacity. If you need predictable throughput, Dedicated is the go-to. Hosted is easier to start with and we have rate limits/quotas.
[03:41] Priya: Also note that routing policies can fall back to cheaper variants if a primary model is unavailable — that's useful for graceful degradation.
[03:48] Maya: Can we pin versions? We need deterministic outputs per release.
[03:51] Priya: Yes model pinning and rollout strategies (canary, A/B, automatic fallback) are first-class in the console.
[03:58] Evan: Security — can you run in our VPC? KMS integrations?
[04:02] Alex: Private deployment supports VPC and on-prem. For Hosted we do encrypted-at-rest; we also integrate with customer KMS via Private deployments or dedicated Keywrap with HSM in some configurations. We'll share our SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[04:16] Maya: Good. On benchmarks — can you run the pilot against our dataset? We want realistic numbers, not just your internal bench.
[04:22] Priya: Absolutely. For pilots we run both hosted and dedicated runs. We'll need a prompt set and a short script. We'll run throughput and p95 latency, token cost, and quality (ROUGE/F1 where applicable).
[04:35] Alex: I'll add that to next steps.
[04:38] (brief cross-talk)
[04:45] Priya: Back to catalog — here's a model detail page for "OpenSumm-13B" (placeholder name). It has a compatibility matrix row:
[04:55]   - q4_0: supported, recommended for latency-sensitive infra.
[04:58]   - q4_k: supported, slightly higher memory but better quality on NER.
[05:02]   - int8: experimental — not recommended for clinical extraction.
[05:06]   - Sequence length tested up to 4k tokens on A100, beyond that some kernels fall back to slower paths.
[05:13] Maya: Do you publish kernel-level notes? We have long templated notes and want to avoid OOM surprises.
[05:19] Priya: Yes, compatibility matrix lists known kernel fallbacks, and we flag models with sequence-length regressions. We also include recommended batch sizes for 500-token and 2k-token distributions.
[05:30] Evan: How do you handle caching — prefix/KV caching? We do many follow-ups and reuse contexts.
[05:35] Priya: Redwood supports KV caching and prefix cache. The console shows expected cache hit rates based on sequence reuse and suggests caching TTLs. That can dramatically reduce per-token cost for your follow-ups.
[05:48] Maya: Important for us. For redaction, do you provide any built-in PII tooling or do we need custom post-process?
[05:54] Priya: We have a plugin-style post-process where you can plug your PII detector; we also ship example pipelines for redaction and differential privacy hooks. But sensitive data should be handled in Private/Dedicated for compliance.
[06:07] Lara: If we do dedicated, is the control plane still Redwood or fully customer-managed?
[06:11] Alex: Control plane is private for our Private offering; Dedicated can be hosted with customer VPC peering or private control plane options. We'll detail the architecture in a follow-up doc.
[06:22] Maya: Okay, can you show the benchmark UI?
[06:25] Priya: Sure. This is our benchmark run page. You can upload a CSV of prompts, pick models from the catalog, and select hardware profiles. We provide p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and quality metrics.
[06:40] Priya: Example run: OpenSumm-7B q4_0 on A10G: p95 latency ~480 ms for 500-token average, throughput ~15 tokens/sec under small batching. Cost estimate $0.004 per 1k tokens (placeholder). OpenSumm-13B q4_k on A100: p95 ~820 ms, throughput ~8 tokens/sec, cost higher.
[06:58] Evan: Those numbers are helpful. For our SLA- we want p95 under 1s for most requests. Seems feasible with 13B on dedicated?
[07:05] Priya: Yes on dedicated you're more likely to meet p95 targets consistently, with reserved capacity. Hosted can hit targets but is subject to multi-tenant variance; we have SLA-backed tiers for higher plans.
[07:17] Maya: What about tokenization differences? We saw differences between models causing token count variance and cost spikes.
[07:23] Priya: We include the tokenizer type and expected tokens per 1k words metric on the model card. Also recommend normalizing prompts.
[07:29] Alex: Quick note — some transcription errors in our shared materials may call out model names incorrectly; we'll ensure the follow-up has corrected names and a compatibility matrix in spreadsheet form.
[07:39] (10 second pause)
[07:50] Maya: Can you talk about regression detection — how do you monitor quality after rollouts?
[07:55] Priya: Redwood Optimize ties model metrics to prompt sets. You can create eval suites — if a deployment rollouts results in a drop beyond a threshold, it triggers an alert and can automatically rollback to the previous pinned model. We also store token-level diffs for debugging.
[08:11] Evan: Great. Regarding quantization, you mentioned q4_k — what are the tradeoffs for long-context stability?
[08:17] Priya: q4_k tends to retain more representational fidelity for entity-heavy tasks, so it's better for NER and extraction. But memory usage is slightly higher. For long contexts you should test kernel fallbacks; some kernels are less optimized for q4_k beyond 2k tokens.
[08:33] Lara: On the infra side, do you have pre-built helm charts or terraform for Dedicated/Private?
[08:38] Alex: Yes we provide terraform modules and helm charts for on-prem or Private control plane deployments. We'll attach those artifacts.
[08:47] Maya: If we run the pilot, can you run the same model with different quantization profiles to compare quality vs cost?
[08:53] Priya: Yes that's a standard pilot setup. We'll run, for example, OpenSumm-13B with q4_0, q4_k, and int8 (if available) and produce a quality vs cost sheet.
[09:05] (screen change)
[09:10] Priya: Now here's the exported compatibility matrix in CSV form — columns: model, size, recommended quant, supported kernels, tested sequence lengths, memory per GPU, recommended batch sizes, estimated cost per 1k tokens.
[09:24] Maya: Can you annotate which models are Redwood-verified vs community-sourced? We want reliability.
[09:29] Priya: Yep — verified models have an icon and include fuller benchmark histories; community models may be flagged as less tested.
[09:36] Evan: On integration — is there an SDK for Node?
[09:39] Alex: We have REST and Node/Python SDKs; sample code for streaming, function-like calling, and structured outputs. We'll share quickstart.
[09:47] Maya: How do you handle retry/backoff logic for partial failures? We want deterministic retries to avoid duplicate notes.
[09:52] Priya: The client SDK supports idempotency keys and automatic de-dupe on retries; console shows failed request traces and token-level errors.
[09:59] Evan: Any customer references in healthcare?
[10:02] Alex: We have several health customers (anonymous in public materials) and we'll set up a reference call if needed.
[10:08] Maya: Okay great. Two questions on costs: 1) network egress for Private? 2) long-term model updates and retraining costs?
[10:15] Alex: 1) Egress depends on deployment mode — Private running in your VPC avoids external egress charges for traffic internal to your cloud, but we'll detail network topologies. 2) Redwood doesn't train models in-house for customers; we support fine-tuning and adapters in workflows but costs depend on the chosen provider/workflow; Optimize can recommend cheaper model variants for the same quality in many cases.
[10:36] Priya: We also show model delta-cost over time when you move from hosted to dedicated accounting for reserved capacity.
[10:42] (brief interruption)
[10:50] Maya: If we need an audit trail for PHI access, do you keep token-level logs?
[10:55] Alex: Auditable logs are available in Dedicated and Private modes. For Hosted we retain limited logs per your privacy settings; we can provide SOC2 controls and integration with your SIEM.
[11:07] Evan: Rolling out — timeline? If we start pilot next week what's realistic?
[11:10] Priya: If you provide prompts and sample data this week, we can run bench and quality tests within 7–10 days — pilot results + recommendations typically in 2 weeks.
[11:20] Maya: That works. We'll aim to get the prompt set by Monday.
[11:24] Alex: Great. Any other questions?
[11:27] Lara: One small ask — in the compatibility matrix, can you highlight known regressions with specific kernel+quant combos? Helps us avoid surprises.
[11:33] Priya: Yes we'll flag that.
[11:36] Maya: Okay last one — support model rollouts with canary traffic split percentages?
[11:40] Alex: Yup canary/A-B with gradual ramping and automatic rollback on quality regressions.
[11:45] (short silence)
[11:50] Alex: Cool — recap of next steps: I'll send pricing and SOW draft by Tuesday, Priya will schedule pilot and run the hosted+dedi benchmarks, Maya will share prompts, Lara will share VPC constraints.
[12:04] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks for the walkthrough.
[12:07] Evan: Thanks all.
[12:09] Priya: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links to the compatibility matrix CSV and security docs.
[12:15] Alex: End meeting.

--- End transcript ---

Notes on transcript quality: occasional transcription errors (model names sometimes truncated, 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache'). Some speaker attributions may be approximate as customers spoke over each other in a few places.
